Les effets précis, les limitations et les conditions d'utilisation de ces Listes restent ceux prévus par les mécanismes effectivement disponibles dans MERP-RMU.

La formation de l'Animiste privilégie les compétences liées aux Animaux, à l'Environnement, à l'Herboristerie, aux Premiers soins, à la Perception et aux différentes formes de connaissances naturelles. Le Développement des Points de Puissance et la Manipulation de la Puissance occupent également une place importante dans la progression de cette profession.

Une distinction essentielle doit être maintenue entre l'Animiste et le Drughân. Les deux professions possèdent les mêmes six Listes de sorts de base, mais leur identité et leur formation diffèrent profondément. L'Animiste est un utilisateur pur de Théurgie, accessible selon les traditions culturelles autorisées. Le Drughân est un semi-utilisateur de Théurgie propre aux Drughu, dont les enseignements sont associés aux traditions des Grands Frères, aux tatouages sacrés et aux connaissances particulières de son peuple.

Les Wuitan des Hommes des Bois représentent une tradition culturelle spécifique. Leur magie est traditionnellement chantée ou psalmodiée, et leurs responsabilités comprennent les soins, les rites et la transmission des connaissances. Les développements historiques de cette tradition prévoient la possibilité de remplacer deux Listes de base de l'Animiste par une Liste du Clerc et une Liste du Rôdeur. Cette possibilité doit être appliquée uniquement dans les conditions effectivement prévues par les règles de création et les variantes culturelles disponibles dans MERP-RMU.

Les Urdharkonur des Hommes du Nord urbanisés et des Gramuz constituent une autre expression culturelle de la profession, associée notamment aux saisons, aux troupeaux et aux traditions communautaires.

Il convient de distinguer les éléments directement issus de Tolkien des conventions du jeu. Les traditions de Yavanna, l'existence des Ents, la relation de Radagast avec les animaux et les pouvoirs exceptionnels de Beorn appartiennent aux récits de Tolkien. L'organisation des facultés naturelles en six Listes de sorts, ainsi que les traditions détaillées des Wuitan et des Urdharkonur, relèvent de l'adaptation ludique de la Terre du Milieu.

Les pouvoirs de l'Animiste ne doivent pas être assimilés aux capacités exceptionnelles des Istari, des Ents ou des changeurs de peau. Les relations entretenues avec de tels êtres demeurent soumises à leur nature propre et aux circonstances de la campagne.

Enfin, l'usage de la magie naturelle reste soumis aux règles de l'Ombre et de la Corruption applicables dans MERP-RMU. La Théurgie de l'Animiste n'est pas intrinsèquement corrompue ; les risques dépendent de la nature des pouvoirs, des circonstances dans lesquelles ils sont employés et des règles effectivement prévues par le module.

L'Animiste prend toute sa dimension lorsque ses connaissances du monde vivant contribuent à la survie des communautés, aux voyages et aux choix qui engagent les territoires traversés par les personnages.

Animist

The Lore of the Living World

Spring has returned to the western valleys of Mirkwood. For several days, rain has swollen the streams that descend from the wooded hills towards the Anduin. The families of a small Woodmen's village have begun tending their gardens again, while hunters follow paths left unused throughout the winter. Near the houses, the first buds have appeared on the fruit trees, and the beehives are stirring back to life.

In a house standing apart from the central square, an elderly woman examines the roots of a plant laid out upon a table. Around her, several earthenware vessels hold seeds, dried leaves, and preparations preserved since the previous autumn. Bunches of herbs hang from the ceiling beams alongside small pieces of bark inscribed in the language of her people.

The woman's name is Maerdis. For nearly forty years, she has watched over the families of this village and several neighbouring settlements. The inhabitants seek her help when their animals fall ill, when hunters are wounded, or when difficulties threaten their harvests. They also ask her counsel when unusual events occur, for she knows the ancient traditions and possesses powers that few among her people are capable of wielding.

This morning, two men come to her door. They are leading a young ox that refuses to move forward and continually strains against the rope tied to its halter. The animal belongs to a family whose fields lie near the edge of the forest. Since the previous day it has been trembling, scarcely eating, and growing agitated whenever it is brought back towards the pastures.

Maerdis asks the men to tether it beneath the awning. She examines its limbs, studies its eyes, and checks its breathing. She finds no serious wound, but fine scratches mark the skin near its shoulder. Among its hairs she discovers several greyish strands that cling stubbornly to her fingers.

She questions the two men. The ox escaped from the pasture the previous evening, when the other beasts suddenly fled the shelter of the trees. One of the boys watching over them heard a noise in the branches, then glimpsed a shadow moving above the path. The men had attributed the incident to an ordinary predator.

The old woman places the strands in a small container. She then lays her hands upon the ox's neck and begins to chant a few words in a language the two men have known since childhood. Her voice remains low and steady. Gradually, the animal ceases to pull against its halter, and its breathing grows calmer.

Maerdis returns to the house for a bundle of dried leaves. She prepares an infusion intended to ease the beast's agitation, then asks the men to take her to the pasture.

They leave the village in the middle of the morning. The path crosses a meadow still damp with rain, follows a stream, and passes between tall beeches whose first leaves are beginning to unfold. A few paces from the forest's edge, the woman stops beside a patch of flattened ferns. Above the path, several branches bear strands like those she removed from the ox's coat.

She recognises the traces of a giant spider that has come from the depths of the forest.

The village hunters have encountered such creatures before, but their presence so close to the houses is troubling. Maerdis examines the surroundings, looks for the routes taken by the animals, and instructs the men to warn the families living near the woods. She advises them to abandon this pasture for the time being and establish watches along the paths.

Before leaving, she kneels beside a young tree whose branches have been broken. Her hands slowly follow the wounds in its bark as she murmurs the words of another chant. The damaged tissues begin to close beneath her fingers. When she rises, she has identified the course of an old track that the villagers can use to move their herd away from danger.

That evening, the families gather in the village's great house. Maerdis explains what she has discovered and takes part in the decisions concerning the protection of the pastures. The elders listen attentively. They know that her learning comes from teachings handed down through generations, and that the powers she exercises demand judgement as well as mastery.

Among the Woodmen, a woman such as Maerdis is called a Wita, “She Who Knows”. She belongs to an ancient tradition whose practitioners watch over living creatures, the seasons, and the knowledge upon which their community's prosperity depends.

In other regions of Middle-earth, such practitioners bear different names and exercise their art according to the customs of their people. All belong to the broad tradition of the Animists, whose magic concerns the forces that sustain life.

Guardians of the Living World

The lives of the peoples of Middle-earth remain closely bound to the resources of the natural world. Forests provide timber, plants, and game; rivers offer routes for travel, fishing, and the irrigation of fields; herds sustain many communities. The changing seasons determine the work of farmers, the migrations of animals, and the periods when journeys become difficult.

Some devote their lives to studying these relationships. They learn to recognise useful plants, the behaviour of animals, and the signs that herald changes in the weather. Their knowledge is passed on through everyday practices, the accounts of elders, and experience gained over many years.

The Animist belongs to these traditions, but also possesses a deep knowledge of Channeling. Their powers allow them to influence certain aspects of the living world, establish particular bonds with animals, encourage the growth of plants, or strengthen their own abilities while moving through natural surroundings.

This calling takes different forms from one community to another. An Animist among the Woodmen takes part in seasonal ceremonies and advises families living near the forests. Among the peoples of the Anduin valleys, their knowledge often concerns pastures, domesticated animals, and the plants that grow along the waterways. In the northern regions, they must understand which resources remain available through long winters and the dangers particular to frozen lands.

Their authority rests above all upon experience. The inhabitants recognise the worth of someone who can preserve a herd, find a rare plant, or identify the cause of a disturbing occurrence. Gradually, the Animist comes to occupy a special place within the community, for their decisions directly concern the resources upon which families depend.

Such responsibility requires close knowledge of places and the creatures that inhabit them. Even modest changes may herald serious difficulties: an illness spreading among animals, a spring whose flow is dwindling, or an unfamiliar species appearing near cultivated land. The Animist seeks to understand these events before recommending the measures required.

Their magical powers thus extend experience acquired among people, animals, and plants. Channeling provides extraordinary means of intervention, but their judgement remains grounded in observation and the teachings they have received.

Yavanna and the Ancient Traditions

In the tales of the Eldar, animals and plants hold an essential place in the history of Arda. Among the Valar, Yavanna Kementári, the Giver of Fruits, watches especially over living things that grow and draw sustenance from the earth. The Elves remember her works, from the earliest shaping of the world to the appearance of the great forests that once covered vast regions of Middle-earth.

The Silmarillion recounts Yavanna's concern over the destruction that the Children of Ilúvatar might bring upon the trees. Her conversation with Manwë notably foretells the coming of the Shepherds of the Trees, the Ents, whose presence would help protect certain forests from those who despoil them.

These traditions give the living world a particular significance. Trees have histories, forests preserve the memory of ancient times, and certain creatures possess faculties beyond those of ordinary animals. The relationships between peoples and their surroundings thus form part of the history of Middle-earth itself.

During the Third Age, Radagast the Brown is among the figures most closely associated with knowledge of plants and animals. Dwelling at Rhosgobel, near the western borders of Mirkwood, he maintains particular relations with birds and other wild creatures. Gandalf acknowledges his considerable mastery of shapes and changes of form, as well as his remarkable knowledge of herbs and beasts.

Radagast, however, belongs to the order of the Istari, whose nature and powers surpass those of ordinary practitioners. His life illustrates the heights to which knowledge of the living world may attain, without making him a direct representative of the Animist profession.

Beorn offers another singular example. This man of the Anduin valleys possesses the ability to assume the form of a bear and enjoys extraordinary relations with the animals that live around him. His powers belong to a particular tradition whose origins remain mysterious. Animists from neighbouring communities may admire his knowledge and benefit from his teaching, but their own magic follows different paths.

Human peoples also preserve traditions associated with nature, sometimes transmitted over many centuries. Some particularly honour powers connected with hunting, growth, and the changing seasons. Others give greater importance to the ancestors who taught them about plants, rites, and the practices necessary for life in their lands.

The Animist inherits this knowledge and perpetuates it according to the customs of their people. They may take part in ceremonies, preserve ancient tales, and pass on teachings whose significance reaches beyond their immediate practical value.

The Wuitan of Mirkwood

Among the Animist traditions of Rhovanion, that of the Wuitan is particularly rich. Among the Woodmen, these women exercise an authority founded upon their knowledge, their experience, and their mastery of ancient magical practices.

A Wita generally fulfils several responsibilities within her community. She knows medicinal plants, advises families when difficulties arise, and helps preserve customary practices. Her teachings also concern natural signs, the changing seasons, and the spiritual traditions of the clan.

The Woodmen inhabit a land whose dangers have profoundly marked their history. Mirkwood harbours wild animals, giant spiders, and servants of the Shadow established in certain regions of the forest. Communities along its borders must safeguard their resources while watching the paths that connect them with other peoples.

The Wita contributes to this protection through her knowledge of places and creatures. She knows which plants flourish beneath the great trees, where animals come to drink, and how changes in vegetation may reveal that an unfamiliar influence has taken hold in a region. Her advice sometimes enables hunters to recognise danger before encountering it.

The magic of the Wuitan takes a particular form. Their powers are traditionally accompanied by songs, rhythmic words, or murmured phrases passed down by earlier mistresses. Learning these formulas forms part of their training, alongside the knowledge of plants and ceremonies.

The Woodmen's communities also observe certain practices associated with the renewal of life. The Cult of Growth, known as Alanakyn, encompasses traditions concerning fertility, trees, and natural cycles. Its great ceremonies are infrequent and may bring together several clans in a clearing regarded as sacred.

Among the Valar, these communities particularly honour Araw, their name for Oromë, associated with hunting and the protection of those who travel through the wild lands. The Wita knows the tales and customs attached to these traditions. She may help pass them on without necessarily holding a position equivalent to that of a priest in the organised religions of other peoples.

Yet the daily lives of these women remain deeply rooted in the lives of families. They attend births, treat wounds, prepare remedies, and intervene when the resources of a village are threatened. Their reputations are built over years of service, through the bonds they maintain with several generations of inhabitants.

An elderly Wita may have known the grandparents of those she advises today. She remembers particularly harsh winters, the movement of settlements, and conflicts between clans. This memory allows her to understand the concerns of her community and place present events within the histories of its families.

Learning the Seasons

The Animist's training generally begins in childhood or adolescence, under a master who has recognised particular aptitudes in a pupil. Close attention to animals, an exceptional memory for plants, or a natural ability to understand changes in the surroundings may all favour their selection.

The first years are devoted to ordinary work. The apprentice helps with the harvest, accompanies hunters, and assists in tending gardens and domestic animals. They discover the resources needed for village life, the periods most favourable to certain crops, and the risks associated with changes in the weather.

The master teaches them to recognise plants in their natural habitats. A useful species may look different depending on the age of its leaves or the soil in which it grows. Some plants should be gathered only at a particular time, while others quickly lose their properties once picked. The apprentice learns to distinguish preparations that will keep for several months from those that must be used immediately.

The study of animals follows a similar progression. The young Animist accompanies shepherds and hunters, observes the habits of local species, and learns the signs by which an injury, an illness, or a reaction of fear may be recognised. Wild animals call for particular caution, since their behaviour varies according to the seasons and circumstances.

Knowledge of the environment also plays an important part. The master demonstrates how to recognise a change in the weather, find a spring, identify a passage that has become dangerous, or understand the consequences of an especially harsh winter. Information gathered during journeys supplements the lessons learned in the village.

Magical training is introduced gradually. The pupil learns the disciplines of concentration necessary for Channeling and discovers how to exert an influence upon certain natural forces. The earliest experiments often concern familiar situations, involving domestic animals or cultivated plants. More demanding powers require deeper mastery and an exact understanding of their effects.

Among the Wuitan, this training is accompanied by the transmission of ancient songs and rites. The young woman learns from her mistress the words associated with ceremonies, the tales of the community, and the obligations that accompany her role as a guardian of tradition.

The transmission of knowledge extends beyond magic. An Animist must learn to listen to the inhabitants, understand their needs, and recognise the consequences of their own decisions. Recommending the abandonment of a pasture, forbidding the gathering of a rare plant, or advising that a settlement be moved may provoke serious disagreement. The authority required to make such decisions develops gradually, as the apprentice earns the trust of those around them.

By the end of this training, the young Animist possesses a deep knowledge of their surroundings and of the powers through which they will practise their art. Yet their apprenticeship continues throughout life, for every season, journey, and encounter offers further opportunities to enrich their experience.

Animals and Their Territories

Animals occupy an essential place in the lives of many communities. Herds provide food, wool, and transport, while hunting remains an important resource in forested and mountainous regions. Wild animals may also threaten settlements, especially when severe winters drive them to seek food near villages.

The Animist learns to understand the behaviour of the species that inhabit their territory. They know their feeding habits, breeding seasons, and the circumstances in which they become dangerous. This experience allows them to advise hunters, protect herds, and intervene when a wounded or frightened animal threatens those who approach it.

Animal Mastery extends this knowledge through magic. Certain powers allow the Animist to calm a creature, establish a particular bond with it, or influence its behaviour. Their effectiveness nevertheless depends upon the conditions of each spell, the species concerned, and the situation in which they are employed.

In the Anduin valleys, these abilities are particularly useful to herders and travellers. A terrified horse can endanger an entire convoy; a disordered herd may scatter across dangerous country. An Animist's intervention sometimes prevents considerable losses, especially when the animals have been disturbed by an unusual event.

In the forests, the same knowledge takes on a different significance. Birds, deer, and smaller predators react to changes in their surroundings. Their presence or absence may reveal developments the inhabitants have not yet noticed.

The Animist generally maintains an attentive relationship with animals entrusted to their care. Some creatures grow accustomed to the practitioner’s home and recognise their voice. Others remain wild, even when the Animist has learned to approach them without causing them to flee.

This distinction matters particularly in Middle-earth, where certain species possess extraordinary intelligence or power. The Great Eagles, the Ents, and creatures associated with the ancient forces of the world belong to particular traditions. Their nature requires that their own wills be respected, rather than treating their relations with other peoples as those of ordinary animals.

Herbs, Plants, and Growth

Knowledge of growing things is another foundation of the profession. The Animist learns to recognise medicinal herbs, edible species, and plants whose properties may prove dangerous. They know the conditions required for their growth and the seasons in which they possess the qualities being sought.

In rural communities, this knowledge contributes directly to the subsistence of families. Gardens provide vegetables, fruit, and herbs used throughout the winter. Wild plants supplement stores when harvests are poor. Preserving seeds and tending fruit trees are also important in regions where each season demands long preparation.

Herb Mastery enables the Animist to deepen their ability to find and prepare natural remedies. Injuries, ordinary illnesses, and ailments brought on by living conditions often require preparations whose effectiveness depends upon the quality of the plants employed. Magical powers strengthen this knowledge when used in appropriate circumstances.

This work brings the Animist into contact with healers and practitioners of other medical traditions. Their expertise principally concerns the resources of the plant world and the benefits that may be obtained from them, whereas other professions possess powers directly concerned with repairing the body.

Plant Mastery is a different field. It allows the practitioner to influence certain plants, encourage their growth, or restore damaged parts. Its applications may benefit farming communities and forest dwellers alike.

An orchard struck by a storm, a rare plant threatened with extinction, or trees injured in a fire all offer opportunities to employ these powers. Magic then forms part of the continuing daily work of cultivating the soil, pruning trees, and preserving useful species.

The Animist must also understand the limits of natural resources. Excessive gathering impoverishes some regions; felling too many trees alters the living conditions of animals and inhabitants. The knowledge passed down by elders makes it possible to assess these consequences and recommend practices that preserve the resources needed by future generations.

The Six Paths of the Animist

The Animist's magic rests upon six Base Spell Lists devoted to animals, plants, and natural forces. These disciplines form a coherent body of teaching, founded on knowledge of the living world and the means of establishing particular relationships with it.

Animal Mastery concerns approaching, calming, and influencing living creatures. It allows particular relationships to be established with animals and their behaviour to be altered according to the effects of the spells employed. This path has valuable applications in the care of herds, during journeys, and whenever a community encounters dangerous species.

Herb Mastery deepens the knowledge required to find, prepare, and enhance plant-based remedies. It directly combines magical powers with herbalism, enabling the practitioner to make more effective use of available resources. Animists devoted to healing often place considerable importance upon this discipline.

Nature's Lore allows certain information to be gathered about the environment, its phenomena, and the beings that inhabit it. It supplements ordinary observation with magical means, giving the character a deeper understanding of the natural circumstances they encounter.

Nature's Movement/Senses strengthens certain physical and sensory abilities. Its powers aid the Animist when traversing difficult terrain, searching for a resource, or identifying dangers in the surrounding environment. This discipline is naturally suited to journeys through the wild lands.

Nature's Protection encompasses means of resistance and defence against certain natural dangers. It enables the practitioner to withstand difficult conditions more safely, subject to the limitations of each spell. Animists who accompany expeditions or live in especially hostile regions may attach great importance to it.

Finally, Plant Mastery concerns the growth, restoration, and influence of plants. This path permits intervention in a variety of circumstances, from crops tended by a community to the species found in forests and wilderness.

The six disciplines offer considerable scope for different specialisations. An Animist responsible for safeguarding harvests will deepen their studies of plants and nature. A practitioner living among herders will devote more attention to Animal Mastery, while a traveller may favour powers of perception and protection.

Such specialisation remains closely connected with the character's training. Knowledge gained through study and experience gives meaning to magical powers, whose use always depends upon circumstances and the practitioner's personal mastery.

Rites and the Passing Seasons

In many communities, the Animist's knowledge is accompanied by participation in traditional ceremonies. The changing seasons, harvests, births, and events affecting natural resources hold particular importance in the lives of families.

Rites take different forms among different peoples. Some accompany agricultural work with song; others hold ceremonies near an ancient tree or a spring considered important to the community. Elders pass down the words, gestures, and customs associated with these gatherings.

The Animist sometimes serves as guardian of this memory. They know when the celebrations are held, the stories that explain their origins, and the commitments that families renew upon these occasions.

Among the Woodmen, the Wuitan play a particular role in rites associated with the renewal of life. The ceremonies of the Cult of Growth are occasions when several families may gather to recall their shared traditions and prepare for the work of the coming seasons.

These practices have a value beyond their magical aspect. They bring communities together, transmit knowledge essential to everyday life, and preserve bonds between families that may live far apart.

The Animist's responsibility is therefore as much to preserve customs as to understand the changes affecting the community. Some ancient ceremonies must be adapted when families move or the resources of a territory change. The resulting disagreements may set generations against one another, particularly when necessity demands the abandonment of places to which the inhabitants are deeply attached.

An experienced Animist takes part in such decisions with the knowledge of those who came before and an understanding of present conditions. In this way, they help keep alive traditions that have accompanied communities for many generations.

Animists Among the Peoples of Middle-earth

Animist traditions take many different forms throughout Middle-earth.

Among the Woodmen, the Wuitan fulfil several essential functions. Their chanted magic, medical knowledge, and participation in ceremonies give them an important place among families and elders. Life near Mirkwood also calls for constant vigilance against the dangers threatening their communities.

Among the Urbanised Northmen and the Gramuz, certain practitioners are called Urdharkona, or Urdharkonur in the plural. Their traditions remain closely associated with the seasons, animals, and resources necessary for community life. In trading settlements, they may also play a part in relations between families, agricultural activities, and exchanges with the surrounding villages.

The Beornings have a particular relationship with the animals and lands of the Anduin valleys. Their knowledge of herds, pastures, and wild species provides a favourable setting for the training of Animists. Such practitioners may exercise their art among families established near the woods or accompany travellers along the roads crossing their territory.

Among the Lossoth, the Animist's knowledge assumes a form deeply adapted to the climate. Plant resources are limited for much of the year, while animals play an essential role in subsistence. A practitioner of this culture knows the behaviour of northern species, the dangers of cold, and the resources available when conditions grow especially severe.

The Dorwinrim preserve other traditions, associated with the crops, gardens, and plant resources of their country. An Animist may help maintain orchards, safeguard harvests, or prepare remedies. Trade also enables them to discover plants brought from distant lands.

Among the Dúnedain, the profession may draw upon knowledge inherited from Númenor and upon relations maintained with other peoples. An Animist of Gondor will more readily practise their art in rural regions, farming estates, or settlements close to forests. In the North, dispersed communities may preserve particular traditions useful for life in the wild lands.

The Elves possess ancient knowledge of the living world, especially among woodland communities. An Elven Animist may deepen their understanding of the relationships between plants, animals, and seasons, drawing upon teachings handed down over many centuries. The traditions of Mirkwood and Lórien offer such characters a particularly rich setting.

This diversity makes it possible to create Animists whose knowledge and customs differ profoundly. Their identity depends as much upon the traditions of their people as upon the way they choose to practise their art.

The Shadow in the Living Lands

The natural regions of Middle-earth have suffered greatly from war and the advance of the Shadow. Some forests have been ravaged; others have become dangerous to those who pass through them. The servants of Morgoth and Sauron have occupied lands once inhabited, disrupting the relationships between communities and their surroundings.

Mirkwood offers one of the clearest examples of this transformation. Once known as Greenwood the Great, it gradually acquires its ill-omened name as the influence of Dol Guldur and the dangers accompanying it spread through its depths.

To an Animist, these changes have particular significance. Animals abandon certain regions, paths become difficult to follow, and dangerous creatures appear near settlements. Communities must alter their patterns of hunting, gathering, and travel.

The Animist takes part in identifying these threats. Knowledge of the territory enables them to notice changes in vegetation and unusual movements among animals. Channeling also gives them means of gathering certain information, protecting companions, and influencing living creatures when circumstances permit.

Yet danger does not arise solely from the creatures of the Shadow. Wars bring the felling of vast areas of woodland, the destruction of crops, and the abandonment of lands tended for generations. Fires, plunder, and the displacement of populations weaken the communities that depend upon these resources.

The Animist may then become a particularly determined defender of their homeland. Attachment to places known since childhood sometimes gives rise to deep hostility towards those who destroy them. Such anger may be justified, but the choices it inspires must be weighed against their consequences for the beings the practitioner seeks to protect.

Corrupted powers may also seek to turn knowledge of nature towards dangerous practices. The desire to exercise absolute dominion over animals, alter the growth of plants, or subjugate living beings represents a departure from the responsibilities traditionally associated with the profession.

The Animist's power is thus bound to the convictions that guide its use. Knowledge of natural forces grants the means to intervene in the living world; the decisions made determine the practitioner's place in the struggle against the Shadow.

The Animist Through the Ages

The Animist's place depends profoundly upon the period chosen for the campaign.

In the First Age, the great forests of Beleriand provide a natural setting for traditions connected with nature. An Elven Animist may live among the communities of Doriath or the peoples dwelling in wooded regions, while a human practitioner helps preserve the resources upon which the Edain depend. The wars against Morgoth, the migrations, and the gradual destruction of certain regions make their knowledge particularly important. The relationship between peoples and the lands they inhabit forms an essential part of their vocation.

In the Second Age, the Animist finds a place among the communities developing throughout Middle-earth. The vast forests of Rhovanion, the Anduin valleys, and human settlements in the western regions offer many possibilities. Some practitioners help bring lands into cultivation, while others preserve ancient traditions in the face of the arrival of new peoples. Relations between the Númenóreans and local populations may also encourage exchanges of knowledge, but can provoke conflicts when the exploitation of resources profoundly transforms the land.

In the Third Age, the profession acquires some of its most characteristic expressions. The Wuitan of the Woodmen, the Urdharkonur of the Northmen, and practitioners among rural communities preserve knowledge adapted to their surroundings. The advance of the Shadow in Mirkwood and the wars affecting neighbouring regions make their responsibilities especially important. Animists must safeguard resources, recognise dangers, and contribute to the survival of communities that are sometimes isolated.

In the Fourth Age, the fall of Sauron makes it possible to envisage a profound transformation of certain regions. Mirkwood becomes Eryn Lasgalen, the Wood of Greenleaves, and neighbouring communities may resume activities that have long been threatened. Abandoned lands are gradually settled once more, while exchanges between peoples encourage the transmission of knowledge. An Animist may help restore gardens and forests, accompany the founding of new villages, or preserve places remembered by their people.

Each Age thus gives the character a particular identity. An Animist of the First Age may know the great forests of Beleriand before their disappearance; one of the Second Age witnesses the expansion of peoples and the transformation of their lands. In the Third Age, the practitioner often protects communities threatened by the Shadow, while a successor in the Fourth Age helps renew the land and the traditions bound to it.

Leaving the Community

The Animist's vocation remains closely tied to the communities and territories in which they received their training. Leaving them is therefore an important decision, generally prompted by a particular necessity or a pursuit that cannot be undertaken among their own people.

Some embark upon a journey to find a rare plant, seek a remedy, or discover the cause of a phenomenon threatening their people's resources. Others seek a master whose knowledge might complete their own education, particularly when an ancient tradition risks disappearing for lack of new pupils.

Circumstances may be more painful. War has destroyed the lands where the character grew up; an exceptionally harsh winter has forced the community to move; a disease has devastated the herds upon which several families depended. The Animist then leaves home to seek new resources or discover knowledge capable of preventing a similar disaster.

Some departures also arise from disagreement with the elders. A young practitioner wishes to share knowledge reserved for a few families, while a Wita hopes to establish relations with communities her mistresses regarded with suspicion. Travel then becomes a way of exploring other traditions and deciding what place the practitioner wishes to occupy among their own people.

Life on the roads imposes conditions unlike those of home. Plants known since childhood become scarce, animals display unfamiliar behaviour, and the seasons do not unfold in quite the same way everywhere. The character must learn to observe new environments and recognise the limits of their knowledge.

Within a company of adventurers, these skills have many applications. The Animist helps find food, recognise natural dangers, and preserve the resources needed for the journey. Their powers facilitate certain dealings with animals, strengthen companions' abilities, and permit intervention upon plants in appropriate circumstances.

Encounters with other practitioners gradually enrich their experience. A Ranger teaches them the ways of the roads and methods of keeping watch; a Lay Healer shares medical knowledge; a Drughân reveals traditions particular to the Drughu. Such exchanges deepen bodies of knowledge that can differ greatly despite their common roots in the natural world.

The experience of travel also transforms the Animist's relations with other people. Accustomed to advising a community whose families they have known for many years, the practitioner now encounters companions who share neither their beliefs nor their customs. Trust is then built through decisions made together and attention paid to one another's difficulties.

Upon returning, the character brings new knowledge, stories, and sometimes practices from which the community may benefit. Yet they also find places that have continued to change in their absence. Harvests have come and gone, children have grown, and some elders have died. Their experience now allows them to regard these changes with an understanding enriched by the lands they have travelled.

Playing an Animist

The Animist offers the opportunity to portray a character whose knowledge and magic are devoted to living beings and the relationships binding them to their environment. Their cultural background, training, and entrusted responsibilities nevertheless determine how they fulfil this calling.

A young Wita of the Woodmen may have grown up under the guidance of a respected mistress, learning the chants needed for healing and the traditions associated with the Cult of Growth. An Urdharkona of the Gramuz may possess a deep knowledge of herds and seasons, while a Lossoth Animist has devoted their youth to understanding the resources of frozen regions. A practitioner from Dorwinion may tend gardens and orchards containing plants from many lands.

The character's relationship with their master is an important part of their story. Did they receive demanding instruction from a renowned elder? Is there a plant they have sought for several years? Has a community entrusted them with protecting a particular place? Have they already witnessed the destruction of a forest or herd they believed they could preserve?

Their character will depend greatly on their experience. Some Animists develop considerable patience, accustomed as they are to observing changes that unfold with the seasons. Others become particularly demanding towards those who exploit resources without regard for the consequences. Trust in tradition may also make it difficult to accept unfamiliar practices, even when their advantages are clear.

Their relationship with magic deserves particular attention. One character may regard their powers as teachings passed down by the elders, accompanied by ceremonies and words whose customary use they observe with care. Another sees magic as a discipline grounded in observation and understanding of natural forces. These views may coexist within a single community and give rise to particularly rich exchanges.

The profession is well suited to campaigns devoted to travel, wild lands, isolated communities, and the consequences of the Shadow for inhabited territories. It also offers many possibilities in adventures where characters must preserve a resource, understand a natural phenomenon, or establish relations with peoples whose traditions differ from their own.

Over the course of life, the Animist will learn that the forces sustaining life are deeply bound to the choices made by the peoples of Middle-earth. The knowledge they pass on, the lands they help preserve, and the relationships they form with their companions will give their calling a meaning that extends beyond the exercise of magical powers.

Gamemaster's Notes — The Animist in MERP-RMU

The Animist is a pure user of Channeling, specialising in natural forces, animals, plants, and the knowledge required for life in the wild lands.

Their prime characteristics are Intuition (In) and Memory (Me). Intuition is also the realm characteristic for Channeling, while Memory represents the breadth of knowledge acquired concerning plants, animals, seasons, and natural traditions.

The Animist has six Base Spell Lists:

Spell ListDomain
Animal MasteryCalming, approaching, and influencing animals
Herb MasteryFinding, preparing, and enhancing plant-based remedies
Nature's LoreGathering information about the environment and natural phenomena
Nature's Movement/SensesEnhancing certain physical and sensory abilities
Nature's ProtectionResistance and protection against certain natural dangers
Plant MasteryGrowth, restoration, and influence of plants

The precise effects, limitations, and conditions of use of these Lists remain those provided by the mechanics actually available in MERP-RMU.

The Animist's training favours skills relating to Animals, the Environment, Herbalism, First Aid, Perception, and various forms of natural lore. Power Point Development and Power Manipulation also play an important role in this profession's advancement.

An essential distinction must be maintained between the Animist and the Drughân. The two professions possess the same six Base Spell Lists, but their identities and training differ profoundly. The Animist is a pure user of Channeling, available according to the permitted cultural traditions. The Drughân is a semi-user of Channeling specific to the Drughu, whose teachings are associated with the traditions of the Great Brothers, sacred tattoos, and the particular knowledge of their people.

The Wuitan of the Woodmen represent a specific cultural tradition. Their magic is traditionally sung or chanted, and their responsibilities encompass healing, rites, and the transmission of knowledge. Historical developments of this tradition provide for the possibility of replacing two of the Animist's Base Lists with one Cleric List and one Ranger List. This option must be applied only under the conditions actually provided by the character creation rules and cultural variants available in MERP-RMU.

The Urdharkonur of the Urbanised Northmen and Gramuz constitute another cultural expression of the profession, associated in particular with the seasons, herds, and community traditions.

Elements drawn directly from Tolkien must be distinguished from conventions introduced by the game. The traditions concerning Yavanna, the existence of the Ents, Radagast's relationship with animals, and Beorn's extraordinary powers belong to Tolkien's tales. The arrangement of natural abilities into six Spell Lists, together with the detailed traditions of the Wuitan and Urdharkonur, belongs to the roleplaying adaptation of Middle-earth.

The Animist's powers must not be equated with the exceptional abilities of the Istari, Ents, or skin-changers. Relations with such beings remain subject to their particular natures and the circumstances of the campaign.

Finally, the use of natural magic remains subject to the rules of Shadow and Corruption applicable in MERP-RMU. The Animist's Channeling is not inherently corrupt; the risks depend upon the nature of the powers, the circumstances in which they are used, and the rules actually implemented in the module.

The Animist comes fully into their own when their knowledge of the living world contributes to the survival of communities, to journeys, and to choices affecting the lands through which the characters travel.
